This page corresponds to the exact occupation U.S. O*NET/SOC 29-2092.00 "Hearing Aid Specialists" (Hearing Aid Specialists): select and fit hearing aids for customers, administer and interpret tests of hearing, assess hearing instrument efficacy, and take ear impressions and prepare, design, and modify ear molds. Official scope text: Select and fit hearing aids for customers. Administer and interpret tests of hearing. Assess hearing instrument efficacy. Take ear impressions and prepare, design, and modify ear molds. The core tasks listed by O*NET include: training customers to use hearing aids or other assistive communication devices (importance 96); counseling clients and their families on communication strategies and the effects of hearing loss (95); selecting and administering tests to evaluate hearing or related disabilities (94); administering basic hearing tests including air conduction, bone conduction, or speech audiometry (93); maintaining or repairing hearing aids or other communication devices (91); administering basic screening procedures including pure tone screening, otoacoustic emissions screening, acoustic immittance screening, and examining the ear canal using otoscopy (91); taking or modifying ear impressions for ear molds and hearing aid shells (86); reading the latest literature and talking with colleagues and attending professional organizations or conferences to keep up with developments in audiology (75); demonstrating assistive listening devices (ALDs) to clients (67); assisting with audiological procedures (such as real-ear measurements, speech audiometry, auditory brainstem response, electronystagmography, and cochlear implant mapping) under the supervision of an audiologist (84); and diagnosing and treating hearing or related disabilities under the supervision of an audiologist (82). Common job titles include Audioprosthologist and Hearing Aid Consultant and Hearing Aid Specialist and Hearing Care Practitioner and Hearing Care Specialist and Hearing Instrument Dispenser and Hearing Instrument Specialist (HIS) and Hearing Specialist and Licensed Hearing Instrument Specialist (Licensed HIS) and National Board Certified Hearing Instrument Specialist (National Board Certified HIS). Scope note: the U.S. wage and employment and industry data presented by O*NET on the 29-2092.00 page are not marked as taken from a parent occupation, so this page labels them faithfully according to this occupation's own scope (29-2092.00); the page also shows a projected 2024—2034 growth of "Much faster than average (7% or higher)" (much faster than average) and marks it Bright Outlook (good prospects). Scope and boundaries are described in the sections below.

Exercise prompt | A completely fictional hearing assessment and hearing aid fitting task package (for practice workflow only; it does not represent any real institution, client, patient, or data). Write a draft plan: (1) how, based on a fictional referral form along with hearing test results and the client's chief complaint, to arrange a fitting in a structured way (client and hearing status, needs and situation identification, administering and interpreting hearing tests, hearing aid selection and fitting and adjustment, real-ear and efficacy verification, ear impression and ear mold and shell fabrication, use and maintenance training, follow-up and review, and records and files), and state which information is insufficient and needs to be supplemented (otologic and medical history and contraindications, type and degree of hearing loss, ear canal and ear impression status, work and life listening situations, dexterity and cognitive and language abilities, and equipment and insurance and cost requirements); (2) how to design the completion and review points for a fictional fitting and adjustment and follow-up record table (fields and definitions, client and ear side, tests and selection and parameters, verification and efficacy, exceptions and review and corrections, and original records and revision audit trails); (3) how to write a handover-ready fitting summary (client—needs and basis—tests and selection—fitting and adjustment and verification—use and maintenance—follow-up and open items); (4) how to record and preserve client hearing and health information and device records, and distinguish disclosable information from controlled materials or materials involving the client's personal health information; (5) how to pause, review, refer, and escalate upon finding otologic abnormalities or indications for medical referral or exceeding the position's authorization or device safety problems. Answer using public materials and simulated data; do not use any real client or patient data.

Fit signals | The work activity importance scores for U.S. O*NET 29-2092.00 show that Assisting and Caring for Others (92), Getting Information (84), Performing for or Working Directly with the Public (84), Working with Computers (83), Updating and Using Relevant Knowledge (82), Identifying Objects, Actions, and Events (79), Documenting/Recording Information (78), Establishing and Maintaining Interpersonal Relationships (78), Making Decisions and Solving Problems (76), and Influencing or Persuading Others (75) are the most important activities for this occupation; the work context (percentage response scope) shows dealing with external customers or the public 90% extremely important, electronic mail 87% every day, contact with others 68%, frequency of decision making 78% every day, indoors, environmentally controlled 92% every day, telephone conversations 78% every day, decision freedom 54% a lot of freedom, importance of being exact or highly accurate 41% extremely important, work with a work group or team 53% extremely important, and work schedule 99% regular. If you are willing to keep communicating with clients who have hearing impairment and make testing and fitting and adjustment solid, can maintain professional judgment between sales and service and medical boundaries, and are willing to take responsibility for clients' hearing and safety and privacy, the daily requirements of this occupation are closer to the way you work.

Caution signals | O*NET also shows (29-2092.00, work activity importance scope and work context percentage response scope): Assisting and Caring for Others (92), Getting Information (84), and Performing for or Working Directly with the Public (84) are the highest activities; dealing with external customers or the public 90% extremely important; electronic mail 87% every day, telephone conversations 78% every day, face-to-face discussions 63% every day; importance of being exact or highly accurate 41% extremely important and 23% important; time pressure 67% once a week or more; conflict situations 19% every day and 30% once a week or more; dealing with unpleasant or angry or discourteous people 41% once a week or more and 26% once a month or more; consequence of error 18% very serious and 63% fairly serious; responsibility for others' health and safety 22% extremely high; exposure to disease or infections 45% once a week or more; and level of competition 19% extremely competitive and 22% highly competitive. This occupation takes hearing testing and hearing aid fitting and adjustment and sales as its subject matter, and a single testing or interpretation error, a single improper selection or adjustment parameter, a single error in making an ear impression or ear mold or shell, a single improper after-sales maintenance or repair, or a single instance of out-of-bounds diagnosis or treatment or delayed medical referral can all damage clients' hearing and ear canals and cause device unusability and trust and compliance risk. O*NET places this occupation in Job Zone Three (medium preparation needed, SVP 6.0 to less than 7.0); the education section of that page shows 44% doctoral degree, 22% high school diploma or equivalent, and 12% postsecondary certificate; in the United States, fitting hearing aids usually also requires meeting the licensing or registration requirements of the state or region. If you find it hard to keep communicating with clients who have hearing impairment, hard to bear the dual pressure of sales and service and medical boundaries, or unwilling to take responsibility for device safety and medical referral judgments, you should treat these as real costs that need careful weighing.

Ownership judgment | Real fit comes from whether you can do three things at once on the same fitting task: do the profession properly (based on hearing tests and client needs, complete selection and fitting and adjustment and verification and ear mold fabrication, and produce usable testing and fitting and follow-up records), keep boundaries and compliance under control (work and keep an audit trail in line with scope of practice and device and medical referral and privacy requirements; distinguish disclosable information from controlled materials or materials involving the client's personal health information and handle them according to policy; and do not diagnose or treat without qualifications or delay referral when there are indications for medical referral), and take on definable position responsibility (be accountable for the testing and fitting and adjustment and device maintenance and records you personally perform, and refer matters beyond the scope of practice or involving medical diagnosis and treatment and medication to the appropriate position or institution according to policy). It is recommended to test this with one verifiable experience (completing a hearing test and fitting plan and a fitting and follow-up record note for a fictional client, or a retrospective review of handling one otologic abnormality or referral risk) rather than relying only on the conclusions of an interest questionnaire.

Direct answer | The "Hearing Aid Specialists" on this page is the exact occupation O*NET 29-2092.00 (Hearing Aid Specialists), and the work can be divided into several categories: first, hearing testing and screening — administering and interpreting tests of hearing (importance 94), administering basic hearing tests such as air conduction, bone conduction, or speech audiometry (93), administering basic screenings such as pure tone screening and otoacoustic emissions screening and acoustic immittance screening and examining the ear canal using otoscopy (91), and assisting with audiological procedures such as real-ear measurements and speech audiometry and auditory brainstem response and electronystagmography and cochlear implant mapping under the supervision of an audiologist (84); second, hearing aid selection and fitting — selecting and fitting hearing aids for customers, and completing selection and adjustment and real-ear and efficacy verification based on tests and needs; third, ear impressions and ear molds and shells — taking ear impressions and taking or modifying impressions for ear molds and hearing aid shells (86), and preparing, designing, and modifying ear molds; fourth, use and care training — training customers to use hearing aids or other assistive communication devices (96), and demonstrating assistive listening devices to customers (67); fifth, counseling and follow-up — counseling clients and their families on communication strategies and the effects of hearing loss (95), and assessing hearing instrument efficacy and following up and adjusting and reviewing; sixth, maintenance and repair and professional development — maintaining or repairing hearing aids or other communication devices (91), and reading the latest literature and talking with colleagues and attending professional organizations or conferences to keep up with developments in audiology (75), and diagnosing and treating hearing or related disabilities under the supervision of an audiologist (82). Work cycle links: reception and needs identification—hearing testing and interpretation—selection and fitting and adjustment—real-ear and efficacy verification—ear impression and ear mold and shell fabrication—use and maintenance training—follow-up and review and recording. This page does not conflate this occupation with adjacent ones such as orthotists and prosthetists, ophthalmic medical technologists and technicians, medical assistants, dental assistants, or speech-language pathology assistants, nor does it expand fitting duties to the point of replacing the medical diagnosis and treatment scope of otolaryngologists and audiologists.

Mainland China scope and gaps | In mainland China, there are positions in hearing aid fitting and hearing rehabilitation and hearing health services that are similar to Hearing Aid Specialists (such as hearing aid fitters, hearing rehabilitation technicians, and audiology-related service personnel); their work and qualifications and standards and records are governed by the Law of the People's Republic of China on the Protection of Persons with Disabilities, the Basic Medical and Health Promotion Law of the People's Republic of China, the Regulations on the Supervision and Administration of Medical Devices, and the Metrology Law of the People's Republic of China, as well as standards and occupational qualification requirements related to hearing aid fitting and hearing health services: matters involving otologic disease diagnosis and treatment and medication must be carried out by medical institutions and personnel with the corresponding qualifications; the selection and adjustment and after-sales service of hearing aids as medical devices must meet product quality and metrology and safety requirements; and client hearing and health information must be protected in accordance with the law and handled under the minimum necessary principle. However, public occupational statistics have not established a national occupational wage distribution precisely corresponding to U.S. O*NET 29-2092.00 (Hearing Aid Specialists): the National Bureau of Statistics publishes average wages of urban unit employees by industry category, which is an industry scope that does not distinguish occupations and does not list this occupation separately. Under the evidence policy, this page only registers the statistical scope and the visible gaps (marked "Evidence insufficient:") and does not use industry averages, job posting offers, or cross-jurisdiction extrapolation from U.S. wages for starting salaries, medians, or personal income; the two sets of scope, China and the United States, differ in legal environment and statistical period, and are not combined or converted.

Ethics and privacy note | Organize work according to scope of practice and device safety and client privacy requirements: hearing testing and selection and fitting and adjustment must be consistent with test results and client needs and current standards and must state their sources and limitations, and must not replace otologic disease diagnosis and treatment and medication or medical decisions; client hearing and health information must follow the principles of informed consent and minimum necessary and purpose limitation; testing and fitting and device records must be accessed, stored, and shared in accordance with institutional and legal requirements; otologic abnormalities or indications for medical referral must be referred according to standards and documented; and upon finding indications for medical referral or device safety problems or exceeding the scope of practice or an ethics conflict, work must pause immediately and be referred and reported according to policy. The content on this page does not constitute any medical, diagnostic, treatment, medication, or legal advice.

Standards and quality boundaries | This page involves three types of requirements: first, professional and quality, meaning hearing testing and selection and fitting and adjustment must be carried out in accordance with hearing tests and equipment standards and scope of practice, with testing and fitting and follow-up and device records kept; second, ethics and privacy and practice boundaries, meaning testing and fitting and counseling must follow the scope of practice and professional ethics, and client hearing and health information must be managed in accordance with institutional and legal requirements, without out-of-bounds diagnosis or treatment; third, records and information, meaning testing and fitting and adjustment and device maintenance records must be truthful, complete, and traceable, and materials that are controlled or involve personal health information and externally disclosed information must be managed according to approval and the minimum necessary principle. This page provides general guidance only and does not constitute medical, diagnostic, treatment, medication, or legal advice.

Recording and collaboration | Record, in accordance with institutional practice and device and data management policies, the reception and needs identification, hearing testing and interpretation, selection and fitting and adjustment, real-ear and efficacy verification, ear impression and ear mold and shell fabrication, use and maintenance training and follow-up and device maintenance and review and referral and original records and revision audit trails, and complete them using the prescribed templates and time limits; upon finding indications for medical referral or device safety problems or a scope-of-practice conflict or inconsistency between records and the actual situation, pause immediately, refer and report according to authorization, and ask superiors and practice regulators to review, and do not modify records without authorization or make retrospective entries.

Boundary conclusion | This page corresponds to O*NET 29-2092.00 (Hearing Aid Specialists), and the core difference from adjacent positions lies in "subject matter, output, and authorization level": this occupation takes client hearing testing and hearing aid fitting and adjustment and ear mold fabrication and follow-up as its subject matter, and its output is hearing testing and fitting and adjustment and verification and follow-up records; Orthotists and Prosthetists (29-2091.00) take the design and fabrication and fitting of orthoses and prostheses as their subject matter; Ophthalmic Medical Technologists (29-2099.05) and Ophthalmic Medical Technicians (29-2057.00) take ophthalmic examinations and diagnostic and treatment assistance as their subject matter; Medical Assistants (31-9092.00) take clinical and administrative assistance as their subject matter; Dental Assistants (31-9091.00) take dental diagnostic and treatment assistance as their subject matter; and Speech-Language Pathology Assistants (31-9099.01) take speech and language therapy assistance as their subject matter. Subject matter, output, and authorization level all differ, and the authority for otologic diagnosis and treatment and medication and medical decisions cannot be carried over across positions.

Core concept of adjacent positions | Positions in the same group and adjacent positions mostly aim to "bring testing, fitting, or assistance services to the prescribed state within the scope of practice and device and ethics boundaries and leave an audit trail," differing in subject matter, output, and authorization level: some take hearing testing and hearing aid fitting and ear molds as their subject matter, and some take orthoses and prostheses or ophthalmic examinations or clinical and dental assistance or speech therapy assistance as theirs.

Core purpose of this occupation | Taking client hearing status and listening needs and devices and standards as its subject matter, complete the work within the scope of practice and ethics and device safety: reception and needs identification, hearing testing and interpretation, selection and fitting and adjustment, real-ear and efficacy verification, ear impression and ear mold and shell fabrication, and use and maintenance training and follow-up and recording, so that clients' hearing needs are addressed, testing and fitting and records are traceable, client information security is controlled, and responsibility boundaries can be explained.

Boundaries of conclusions for this occupation | Hearing testing and fitting conclusions state only verifiable tests and needs and selection and adjustment and results and records, and distinguish measured facts from judgment inferences and items pending verification; unauthorized judgments and commitments must not be made on matters beyond one's own authorization (otologic disease diagnosis and treatment, medical referral and medical decisions, handling and disclosure of client health information); when indications for medical referral or device safety problems or a scope-of-practice conflict arise, or when records and the actual situation are inconsistent, work must pause and be escalated or referred or handed over, and conclusions must also be able to withstand review by superiors and by practice regulators and regulatory inspection.

Pre-onboarding verification note | The following six items are for item-by-item verification before applying and onboarding, to avoid inferring actual duties and authorization from job titles or promotional language; verification results should be based on written recruitment information and the employment contract and the position description and practice and data policy documents, and should be continuously confirmed after onboarding. This page lists verification directions only and does not constitute a formal conditions checklist for any institution or position. Special note: in the United States this occupation falls under O*NET Job Zone Three (medium preparation needed, SVP 6.0 to less than 7.0), and the education section shows 44% doctoral, 22% high school, and 12% postsecondary certificate; in the United States, fitting hearing aids usually also requires meeting the licensing or registration requirements of the state or region (such as a Hearing Instrument Specialist license) and may require certification from the National Board for Certification in Hearing Instrument Sciences; in mainland China, positions involving hearing aid fitting often have education and occupational qualification and device and metrology requirements, so be sure to confirm the position's specific requirements for education and training and licensure and certification and continuing education and the handling of client information and position authorization.

Preface | The following comparison is organized in four columns: "career direction—core work and output—key differences—who it suits better." Hearing aid fitting and orthotic and prosthetic fitting and ophthalmic examination and clinical and dental assistance and speech therapy assistance are often connected within the same health or rehabilitation system, but connection does not mean they are interchangeable; when choosing across directions, you should relearn that direction's subject matter and standards and data and authorization and responsibility boundaries.

Key differences: this occupation takes client hearing testing and hearing aid fitting and adjustment and ear mold fabrication and follow-up as its subject matter, and, drawing on audiology and hearing aid fitting and device knowledge and scope of practice, completes testing and selection and adjustment and verification and recording within authorization, being responsible for clients' hearing and device safety and privacy; the other positions center respectively on orthotic and prosthetic fitting, ophthalmic examination and diagnostic and treatment assistance, clinical and administrative assistance, dental diagnostic and treatment assistance, or speech and language therapy assistance, and each usually has more specialized standards and qualifications and subject matter, and none bears primary responsibility for hearing aid fitting and follow-up (though they must collaborate with this occupation and clearly define boundaries).

Better suited to people who are willing to keep communicating with clients who have hearing impairment over the long term, can maintain professional judgment between sales and service and medical boundaries, and are willing to take responsibility for testing and device safety and privacy.

Core work and output: administer and interpret hearing tests and basic hearing tests and screenings, select and fit hearing aids and adjust and verify them, take ear impressions and prepare and modify ear molds and shells, train customers to use and maintain devices, counsel on communication strategies and follow up and adjust, and maintain or repair devices; the output is hearing testing and fitting and adjustment and verification and follow-up and device records (O*NET/SOC 29-2092.00).

What kind of personality is better suited to being a Hearing Aid Specialist? This occupation values communication and empathy, rigor about practice and devices and precision requirements, a sense of responsibility for client safety and privacy, and stability under sales and after-sales pressure, rather than any particular personality type; the O*NET interest code is SCI (Social—Conventional—Investigative), which can serve as a starting point for exploration.

Are introverts suited to this occupation? Yes. This occupation involves a great deal of testing and adjustment and ear mold fabrication and recording work, and it also requires communicating with clients and teams (dealing with external customers or the public 90% extremely important, electronic mail 87% every day, telephone conversations 78% every day, contact with others 68%).
Introversion and extraversion are not a validated threshold; you can observe client communication and parameter checking, and the predictive validity of personality versus skills is not compared.

Which MBTI type is most suitable for this occupation? No type has been proven most suitable. The MBTI is not an occupational qualification or ability assessment tool, and occupational fit depends mainly on audiology and fitting skills and practice adherence.

Which Holland interest type is more suitable for this occupation? The O*NET interest code is SCI: Social (communicating with and caring for and counseling clients with hearing impairment), Conventional (maintaining order in devices and data and records according to standards and processes and precision requirements), and Investigative (understanding hearing and device problems with evidence and technology); it can be used to explore task preferences, not to predict performance.

No validation research on how personality or interests affect performance in this occupation was obtained, and no individual work performance conclusions are given; learning preparation must be verified separately against professional training and qualifications and real positions.

Can someone who is not good at math do this occupation? Basic test data and device parameter and result interpretation and statistics abilities are needed; a quantitative foundation can be filled in through training and tool support, but a complete inability to adapt to data and device adjustment would be clearly limiting.

Does this occupation require high emotional intelligence? It requires emotional stability and empathy and communication and conflict handling skills, but no specific assessment scores. Client objections and after-sales and sales pressure require self-regulation and communicating and reporting according to procedure.

Can the Enneagram be used to judge whether I am suited? No. The Enneagram is a self-exploration tool and does not constitute a conclusion about occupational ability or fit; judging fit should look at whether you can complete hearing testing and fitting and follow-up work under practice and privacy and device requirements.

How can I use deliverables to judge which direction suits me? Use one real or simulated fitting task to test: whether you can complete a hearing test and fitting plan and a fitting and follow-up record note, or whether you can complete a retrospective review of handling one medical referral or device safety risk; such evidence explains fit better than a questionnaire.

Direct answer | The core risk of this occupation is not whether the device can be sold, but four types of high-consequence failure: fitting and safety failure (improper hearing testing or interpretation or selection or fitting and adjustment or ear impression and ear mold fabrication, or involvement in otologic disease diagnosis and treatment and medication, or delayed referral when there are indications for medical referral, which may damage clients' hearing and ear canals and make devices unusable and create trust and compliance risk), privacy and ethics failure (improper handling of client hearing and health information or missing informed consent or out-of-bounds sharing, which may cause privacy leaks and practice and compliance and legal risk), quality and record failure (distorted or version-uncontrolled testing or fitting or adjustment or after-sales or device or inventory and sales records, which may cause inaccurate fitting and misjudgment of traceability and performance and compliance), and authorization and collaboration failure (making medical judgments beyond the scope of practice or delaying referral or external disclosure, critical audiology or ear mold fabrication or after-sales capability resting on a single point, and unclear standards with otology and audiology and manufacturers and regulators on scope and responsibility and disclosure and recall boundaries leading to disputes). items.title: Education, training, and qualifications: which are the real thresholds for this occupation?

paragraphs: Qualification boundary one | Job requirements, education, proof of training, fitting licensure or registration in the state or region and specialized certification and continuing education, health and occupational health examinations, institutional and position authorization, and testing and fitting and disclosure authority are different states: meeting hiring requirements does not equal obtaining the authority to independently carry out fitting or issue testing and fitting conclusions. entries.answer: The Hearing Aid Specialists on this page is the exact occupation O*NET 29-2092.00 (Hearing Aid Specialists): select and fit hearing aids for customers, administer and interpret tests of hearing, assess hearing instrument efficacy, and take ear impressions and prepare, design, and modify ear molds. Core tasks include training customers to use hearing aids or other assistive communication devices (importance 96), counseling clients and their families on communication strategies and the effects of hearing loss (95), selecting and administering tests to evaluate hearing or related disabilities (94), administering basic hearing tests such as air conduction and bone conduction and speech audiometry (93), maintaining or repairing hearing aids or other communication devices (91), administering basic screenings such as pure tone screening and otoacoustic emissions screening and acoustic immittance screening and examining the ear canal using otoscopy (91), taking or modifying ear impressions for ear molds and hearing aid shells (86), assisting with real-ear measurements and speech audiometry and auditory brainstem response and electronystagmography and cochlear implant mapping under the supervision of an audiologist (84), and diagnosing and treating hearing or related disabilities under the supervision of an audiologist (82). Common job titles include Hearing Aid Specialist and Hearing Instrument Specialist (HIS) and Hearing Instrument Dispenser and Hearing Care Specialist and Hearing Aid Consultant and National Board Certified Hearing Instrument Specialist (National Board Certified HIS); on the 29-2092.00 page, O*NET shows that the main industries for this occupation in the United States are retail trade and healthcare and social assistance. What is described on this page is the U.S. occupational classification scope, and wages and employment follow this occupation's (29-2092.00) own scope; the content on this page does not constitute any medical, diagnostic, treatment, medication, or legal advice.

entries.answer: The core differences lie in subject matter, output, and authorization level: this occupation takes client hearing testing and hearing aid fitting and adjustment and ear mold fabrication and follow-up as its subject matter, and its output is hearing testing and fitting and adjustment and verification and follow-up records; Orthotists and Prosthetists (29-2091.00) take the design and fabrication and fitting of orthoses and prostheses as their subject matter; Ophthalmic Medical Technologists (29-2099.05) and Ophthalmic Medical Technicians (29-2057.00) take ophthalmic examinations and diagnostic assistance as their subject matter; Medical Assistants (31-9092.00) take clinical and administrative assistance as their subject matter; Dental Assistants (31-9091.00) take dental diagnostic and treatment assistance as their subject matter; and Speech-Language Pathology Assistants (31-9099.01) take speech and language therapy assistance as their subject matter. Subject matter and work and authorization level all differ, and the authority for otologic diagnosis and treatment and medication and medical decisions cannot be carried over across positions.

entries.answer: Common failures include: improper hearing testing or interpretation or selection or fitting and adjustment or ear impression and ear mold fabrication, or delayed medical referral, or out-of-bounds diagnosis and treatment; improper handling of client hearing and health information or missing informed consent or out-of-bounds sharing and disclosure; distorted or version-uncontrolled testing or fitting or adjustment or after-sales or device or inventory and sales records, or improper handling of conflicts of interest and sales inducement; making medical judgments beyond the scope of practice or delaying referral or external disclosure; critical audiology or ear mold fabrication or after-sales or fitting capability resting on a single point; and insufficient adaptation of fitting or after-sales or accessibility and language and culture, or insufficient protection of device and ear canal safety. The control points are to verify and review and document according to the scope of practice and device and privacy and informed consent requirements, and to pause and refer and report immediately in the event of otologic abnormalities or indications for medical referral or device safety or scope-of-practice conflicts. subject.name: Hearing Aid Specialists
subject.summary: The Hearing Aid Specialists corresponds to the exact occupation O*NET/SOC 29-2092.00 "Hearing Aid Specialists": select and fit hearing aids for customers, administer and interpret tests of hearing, assess hearing instrument efficacy, and take ear impressions and prepare, design, and modify ear molds; core tasks include training customers to use hearing aids or other assistive communication devices, counseling on communication strategies and the effects of hearing loss, administering and interpreting tests of hearing and basic hearing tests and screenings, taking ear impressions and preparing and modifying ear molds and shells, maintaining or repairing equipment, and assisting with diagnosis and treatment under the supervision of an audiologist; common job titles include Hearing Aid Specialist and Hearing Instrument Specialist (HIS) and Hearing Care Specialist and Hearing Aid Consultant. Official scope text: Select and fit hearing aids for customers. Administer and interpret tests of hearing. Assess hearing instrument efficacy. Take ear impressions and prepare, design, and modify ear molds. Scope note: the U.S. wage and employment and industry data presented by O*NET on the 29-2092.00 page are not marked as taken from a parent occupation, so this page labels them faithfully according to this occupation's own scope (29-2092.00); this occupation is projected to grow 7% or higher over 2024—2034 and is marked Bright Outlook, and O*NET places it in Job Zone Three (medium preparation needed, SVP 6.0 to less than 7.0). The content on this page does not constitute medical, diagnostic, treatment, medication, or legal advice.
